results.title: Determining and reporting minimal important change for patient-reported outcome instruments in pulmonary medicine
results.content: It is impossible to directly capture the internal scales and thresholds patients use to make individualised determinations, but we can indirectly use them to generate estimates for MCIDs. We do so by employing anchor measures: external criterion variables (other PROs or clinical parameters related to the target PRO score), which are collected simultaneously and leveraged to identify patients that have experienced a minimal, meaningful, within-patient change. If we know what a minimal and important change is for the anchor, we can estimate the same for the target PRO by applying anchor-based statistical methods. Core criteria for judging the trustworthiness of a minimal clinically important difference (MCID) estimate for a patient-reported outcome instrument (PRO) [7] and recommendations for studies aiming to generate MCID estimates for PROs in patients with pulmonary conditions. Here, investigators estimate MCIDs by calculating the mean change score for the PRO variable in the subgroup of patients who perceived minimal change over the same time on the anchor. MCID estimates derived using this approach can be supplemented with graphical methods such as the anchor-stratified empirical cumulative density function for the PRO change score [6], which allows comparisons of mean PRO change scores between anchor subgroups (e.g. minimal improvement versus minimal deterioration). In progressive pulmonary fibrosis and other conditions in which HRQoL generally declines over time [9], it is perhaps more reasonable to estimate the MCID for stability; that is, the PRO threshold which separates the cohort into patients that did not worsen on the anchor (i.e. remained stable or improved) and those that worsened (at least minimally or more). Displays of anchor subgroups used in receiver operating characteristic or predictive modelling methods to estimate the minimum important change to the patient for a patient-reported outcome instrument for a) improvement or b) deterioration. Employing a metric like the Reliable Change Index (RCI) could determine whether an individual's PRO change score is statistically significant; pairing RCI results with anchor-based MCID estimates would allow categorisation of patients into those whose change is statistically significant and meaningful, statistically significant but not meaningful, etc. Evaluating the credibility of anchor based estimates of minimal important differences for patient reported outcomes: instrument development and reliability study.

results.title: Understanding the Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID) of Patient-Reported Outcome Measures
results.content: Objective: The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) of a patient-reported outcome measure (PROM) represents a threshold value of change in PROM score deemed to have an implication in clinical management. To define the 3 levels of MCID for avDS, we used an anchor-based method linked to: (1) scales capturing subtle changes in global mobility and motor functions, (2) clinical and health-related measures, and (3) disease-related patient-reported outcomes. The effectiveness of the therapy was assessed based on patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) values, specifically visual analogue scale (VAS), quick version of the disabilities of the arm, shoulder and hand (QDASH), patient-rated tennis elbow evaluation (PRTEE), and the achievement of minimal clinically important difference (MCID). This study aimed to compare the time to reach the minimal clinically important difference for improvement (MCID) for the Hip Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcomes Score-Physical Function Short Form, Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) Global Physical, and PROMIS Physical Function short form 10a (PF-10a). A sensitivity-specificity approach was used to identify the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) for improvement and deterioration for each of the 10 ESAS symptoms.METHODS This multicenter, prospective, longitudinal study enrolled patients with advanced cancer. Score changes in the five different questionnaires were subjected to both distribution- and anchor-based methods: standard error of measurement (SEM) and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves to define clinical improvement. Objective: To assess the usability of Minimal Important Difference (MID) and minimal clinically important difference (MCID) for measuring meaningful changes in disease-specific and generic HRQoL outcomes in patient-centered care. Several studies have investigated whether observed changes are meaningful to patients, using a variety of approaches to estimate the minimum clinically important difference (MCID). Objective To discuss the concepts of the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) and the smallest detectable difference (SDD) and to examine their relation to required sample sizes for future studies using concrete data of the condition-specific Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) and the generic Medical Outcomes Study 36-Item Short Form (SF-36) in patients with osteoarthritis of the lower extremities undergoing a comprehensive inpatient rehabilitation intervention.MethodsSDD and MCID were determined in a prospective study of 122 patients before a comprehensive inpatient rehabilitation intervention and at the 3-month followup.

results.title: Abnormal involuntary movement scale in tardive dyskinesia: Minimal clinically important difference
results.content:
Title: Abnormal involuntary movement scale in tardive dyskinesia: Minimal clinically important difference
Mean changes from baseline in Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale total score were analyzed in all participants (valbenazine- and placebo-treated) with a Clinical Global Impression of Change-Tardive Dyskinesia or Patient Global Impression of Change score of 1 (very much improved) to 3 (minimally improved). An minimal clinically important difference of 2 points was esti-mated based on least squares mean changes in Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale total score in participants with a Clinical Global Impression of Change-Tardive Dyskinesia score ≤3 at week 6 (mean change: –2.2; median change: –2) or Patient Global Impression of Change score ≤3 at week 6 (mean change: –2.0; median change: –2). The placebo-controlled clinical trials of these drugs had some differences in study design (e.g., treatment duration, eligibility criteria), but both used the Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale (AIMS) 7 to measure the presence, severity, and changes in TD. Along with other analytical approaches (e.g., Cohen ’s effect size, number needed to treat [NNT]), one way to estimate clinical relevance of recent TD trial results would be to identify a minimal clinically important differ-ence (MCID) for the AIMS total score. Estimation of the AIMS MCID was investigated based on participants who had a minimal or better CGI-TD response at week 6 (score ≤3), regardless of treatment, with supporting analyses based on the more stringent CGI-TD response de fi nition (score ≤2) and PGIC responses (score ≤2 or ≤3). Based on participants with a CGI-TD score ≤2 at week 6 (Fig. 4B), the estimated MCID for AIMS total score was 3 points. 17 Based on both clinician- and patient-rated anchors of minimal improve-ment (CGI-TD and PGIC score ≤3 at week 6), mean and median changes in AIMS total score (sum of items 1-7) suggested an MCID of 2 points in adults with TD. However, consistent with the CGI-TD results, MCID estimates based on patient-reported improvements suggest that a 2- to 3-point decrease in AIMS total score may be considered clinically meaningful. In the valbenazine clinical trials, AIMS response was de fi ned a priori as ≥50% total score improvement, 9,10 which is more stringent than the 20% to 40% MCID-based results in the current analysis.
